new_statements.quote: The primary stress pattern in Migabac is word initial with an alternating secondary stress throughout the phonological word. This represents a typical trochaic pattern. … However, this pattern is not entirely consistent. Many times primary stress is found on the second syllable with an alternating secondary stress. … I could not identify a contrast in the number of syllables in a word or in the root, open or closed syllables, or any other feature that would determine whether the first or second syllable received primary stress.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the same source the catalog build used ( classification variable, CONFIRMED), so the reading agrees with the catalog's evidence; note the target dump's catalog_records entry for Migabac carries an EMPTY rule string, which this source fills: default initial/trochaic with unexplained initial-vs-peninitial variation inside a left two-syllable window, plus a penult sub-rule for -ne adjectives. Analysis is of the southern dialect (Kapawa, Daumbole, Butengka) unless stated otherwise.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Headline rule: primary stress on the first syllable with alternating (trochaic) secondary stress rightward, e.g. 312121. The author immediately qualifies it: primary stress is 'many times' on the second syllable instead, the same word can be read with initial stress by one speaker and second-syllable stress by the other, and no conditioning factor (syllable count, open vs closed syllables, root length) could be found. Primary stress stays within the first two syllables. Stress is cued by higher pitch, loudness and duration; word-level stress is explicitly separated from clause-level intonation (rise plus final lengthening at the end of dependent clauses). B-readers tally of the 48-item Long Words list (first reader): 13 initial, 29 second-syllable, 6 third-or-later primary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating secondary stress after the primary through the phonological word (numbers 1/2/3 = unstressed/secondary/primary); 'secondary stress is often obscured on longer words' by intensity lowering after the primary; the alternation is itself sometimes broken (131221, 13112112 patterns), possibly by stress-attracting suffixes, 'a consistent system has not been worked out'.
new_statements.exceptions: Reduplicated two-syllable words typically 1321 (moli-moli 'first'); derived adjectives in -(ŋ)ne consistently have primary stress on the penult, i.e. the syllable immediately before the suffix (131 in three-syllable words, e.g. suŋu-ne 'big'); in serial/compound verb constructions the second root sometimes takes primary stress, analysable as two phonological words; inter-speaker variation initial vs second on the same word; vowel sequences sometimes count as one unit.
new_statements.identity_note: McEvoy 2003/2005 (p. 262): two main dialects, northern (Walingai, Hudewa) and southern (Kapawa, Daumbole, Butengka; Ago close to the southern); 'All analysis in this paper is based on the southern dialect unless otherwise designated.' Data collected 1997-1999 and 2002-2003. The 2008 thesis presumably describes the same variety (same author) but was not opened.

new_statements.quote: The general stress pattern in Migabac is primary stress on the first syllable with an alternating secondary stress that decreases in intensity across the phonological word. However, stress is not always consistent. In a reading test of long words, a variation was found, with some readers placing primary stress on the second syllable, again with an alternating stress pattern. This is found in natural speech as well. Adjectives, which are often three syllables, are consistently stressed on the penultimate syllable. Vowel sequences often function as a unit in the alternating stress pattern.
new_statements.citation: McEvoy, Steve (2008). Grammar of narrative discourse in Migabac. M.

new_statements.relation_note: Same author, explicitly 'summarized from sections of McEvoy (2005)' (the catalog source): initial primary + alternating secondary (trochaic), inconsistency with a second-syllable variant, adjective penult sub-rule -- all already in the catalog record/existing statement (which reads 'unclear or contradictory' / classification variable). Adds only the framing 'general stress pattern' = initial, the remark that the second-syllable variant came from a reading test of long words and also occurs in natural speech, and that all analysis is on the southern dialect. No new stress data; no contradiction.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default (general) pattern: primary stress on the word-initial syllable, then alternating secondary stresses of decreasing intensity across the phonological word (trochaic rhythm); stress is not contrastive. The pattern is not fully consistent: some speakers (reading test of long words, also natural speech) put primary stress on the second syllable with alternation from there. Adjectives (typically trisyllabic) take penultimate stress. Vowel sequences count as one unit for the alternation. The author defers to McEvoy (2005) for evidence; this is a summary, not new analysis.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Alternating secondary stress after the primary, 'decreases in intensity across the phonological word'; vowel sequences often function as a single unit in the alternating count.
new_statements.exceptions: Variation: primary stress on the second syllable for some readers/speakers (with alternating pattern from there), found in natural speech too; adjectives (often three syllables) consistently penultimate.
new_statements.identity_note: Migabac [mpp], Eastern Huon, Morobe Province; the thesis states 'All analysis is based upon the southern dialect' (sect. 2.2, p. 22); phonology summarized from McEvoy (2005).

audit.reasoning: The classification 'variable' (primary stress on one of the first two syllables, default initial with rightward trochaic secondaries, first-vs-second unpredictable and speaker-variable) rests on the only published phonology of Migabac, McEvoy 2005 (SIL Data Papers 47), which we hold; the deciding quotation, the exception quotation and the domain quotation are all verbatim at the cited pages (275-277), and the author explicitly rules out syllable count and syllable weight as conditioners, so the classification faithfully reflects the source. The description is semi-instrumental (Speech Analyzer intensity graphs, two speakers, appendix data), which is as good as SIL sketches get. The only plausibly better source is the same author's 2008 381-page M.A. discourse grammar, which is not openly available (DIU lists it without a PDF, SIL-PNG record empty, the Internet Archive offline/no capture, pnglanguages.sil.org
